blocks.text: Track which elements belong to the same group. Union Find answers "are these two things connected?" in nearly O(1) time the secret weapon behind Kruskal's MST, network connectivity, and cycle detection.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406029061-9107122.png
Three disjoint sets. Every node points to its root.
Same root = same set. find(1) = 3, find(4) = 6, find(7) = 9.
Imagine you have a network of computers. Some are connected, some are isolated. As cables get added, groups merge.
At any point you want to answer: are computer A and computer B in the same connected group?
Union Find (also called Disjoint Set Union DSU) is the data structure built exactly for this.
It maintains a collection of non-overlapping sets and supports two operations union (merge two sets) and find (which set does this element belong to?) in nearly constant time.

CORE IDEAE: Every set is represented as a tree. Each node stores a pointer to its parent. Therootof the tree is the representative (ID) of the set. Two elements are in the same set if and only if they share the same root.
1. find(x)
Returns theroot of x.
Keep going to the parent until a node points to itself.
2. union(x, y)
Joins the sets ofxandy.
Find their roots, then make one root the parent of the other.
CONNECTED CHECK: To check if x and y are in the same set:
find(x) == find(y). If their roots match, they're connected.

blocks.text: Naive Implementation (No Optimisations)
Start simple. Each element is its own parent. find walks up the tree. union joins two roots.
All nodes are connected like a long chain (1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5), so if you try to find the root of node 1, you have to go through every node one by one, which makes it slow and takes O(n) time.
After applying path compression, all nodes directly point to the root (5), so finding the root of any node takes just one step, making it very fast with O(1) time.
The naive version can degrade to O(n) per operation. Two simple techniques fix this entirely and bring both operations to nearly O(1).
OPTIMISATION 1:  PATH COMPRESSION
When you call find(x) and walk up to the root, make every node on that path point directly to the root. Future calls to find on those same nodes become instant.
OPTIMISATION 2: UNION BY RANK
When merging two trees, always attach the shorter tree under the taller one. This keeps trees flat. Store the rank (approximate height) of each tree and always make the higher-rank root the new root.
Full Optimised Implementation
Combining both optimisations gives you the production-ready Union Find this is what you write in every interview and real codebase.
1. Initial State: 4 separate sets, each node is its own root.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406029062-902163916.png
2. union(1,2):  Node 1 becomes root, Node 2 joins it. 3 separate sets remain.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406029062-828071638.png
3. union(2,3) Node 3 also joins Set 1 under root 1. Now 2 sets remain (1,2,3 together and 4 alone).
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406029310-732499308.png
4. union(1,4) Node 4 joins too. All 4 nodes are now in one single set under root 1.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406029310-771769128.png
union operations progressively merge four separate nodes into one set. Root (1) stays flat no long chains.
Time and Space Complexity
With both path compression and union by rank, both operations are effectively constant time.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406029311-337009329.png

WHAT IS Α(N)? α is the inverse Ackermann function. 

It grows so slowly that for any realistic input even n = 10⁸⁰ (atoms in the universe) α(n) ≤ 4. 

For all practical purposes, both operations areO(1).

blocks.text: <hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">
Union Find detects cycles in an undirected graph elegantly. For each edge (u, v): if find(u) == find(v), they're already connected adding this edge creates a cycle. Otherwise, union(u, v).
<hr style="border-width: 1px medium medium; border-style: solid none none; border-color: rgb(224, 224, 224) currentcolor currentcolor; border-image: none; margin: 24px 0px;">

items: Kruskal's MST: Add edges in sorted order. Use Union Find to skip edges that would create a cycle.
Cycle detection: Detect cycles in undirected graphs. Faster and simpler than DFS for this specific task.
Network connectivity: Track connected components dynamically as edges are added to a network.
Number of islands: Classic grid problem union adjacent land cells and count remaining components.
Percolation: Simulate when a system connects top to bottom used in physics and chemistry models.
Friend circles: Group users into friend clusters. Union when two users are connected, count roots for group count.
